167.context: Cesare searches Alexandria's busy harbor for his stolen ship. His experience leads Hodram to recruit him with the prospect of finding it during their travels. Optional ship-buying advice follows, including a separate polite refusal branch. Preserve Cesare's earnest, overformal voice and the exact tutorial facts.
notes: Bind エリュシオン号 to approved ship terminology before drafting; do not invent a replacement ship or completed recovery.
Price categories are the stated approximate thresholds, not an exhaustive invented classification.
Write narrative percent as words in final English; preserve source macros and the one-to-five quantity limit.
meanings: Hodram surveys bustling Alexandria and its many moored ships, then notices something.
A man rejects another possible ship and desperately calls for his beloved エリュシオン号.
Charles wonders whether he is searching for something.
Hodram agrees and asks the man directly.
The man says he is searching for his own ship, エリュシオン号.
Hodram reacts questioningly.
The man and that ship once sailed the seven seas.
Pirates attacked; he survived, but they took the ship.
Charles confirms that this is why he is searching.
He has searched various ports without finding it yet.
Hodram asks whether sailing the seven seas means he has traveled around the world.
He confirms travels through Asia, the New World and many countries.
Hodram asks his shipboard position.
He proudly states that he was the captain.
Hodram weighs the local knowledge and captain's experience.
Proposes that the man join his ship and help with his work.
Traveling around the world together should also offer a chance to find the missing ship.
Charles laughs that he expected exactly such an offer from Admiral {MACRO:FI}.
The man gratefully and eagerly accepts.
Hodram offers to show him aboard, introduces himself as {MACRO:FI} {MACRO:FA} and says he has high expectations.
The man introduces himself as Cesare Tony.
Charles welcomes Cesare and introduces himself as Charles Rochefort.
Cesare asks whether the admiral would hear his opinions about choosing ships.
In the refusal branch, he admires the admiral's independent principles rather than taking offense.
He excuses himself to prepare for departure.
In the advice branch, he begins his explanation.
While merely increasing contracted ports and routes, buying ships is unnecessary: one-percent contracts limit purchases to roughly one to five units of goods.
Once market share grows enough to buy many goods, it is time to acquire ships.
The first considerations are ship size and price.
A ship must match market share and funds; otherwise it demands more sailors without enough available merchandise to fill it.
Price indicates size: below 5,000 is small, 10,000 to 20,000 medium, and above 50,000 large.
Cheap small ships let a fleet increase cargo capacity even with limited funds.
After trading builds up funds, replace them with medium ships.
Medium ships have two or three masts; three are faster but require more sail handlers.
Refitting can provide the maximum five cargo holds; marine quarters and gun batteries are unnecessary if no fighting is planned for the time being.
For long ocean voyages opening distant routes, more supply holds extend sailing range considerably.
Conflict with another faction will make large ships necessary.
At least the flagship should have marine quarters and armed batteries to make naval victories feasible.
Funds remain the constraint: two medium ships are cheaper than one large ship and can carry more merchandise.
Eventually large replacements will be needed, but old medium ships may be worth retaining for future regional fleets.
Concludes the advice and excuses himself to prepare for departure.

168.context: The ship search initially looks hopeless, then Cesare recognizes his former vessel aboard Rafael's fleet. The carved inscription establishes his claim. Cesare declines to deprive them of an indispensable ship, but Rafael returns it despite Claudio's objections. Preserve the mutual generosity, Claudio's practical frustration and Gerhard's admiration; Hodram is not the speaker making Rafael's decision.
notes: Pirates usually abandoning stripped ships is Gerhard's generalization, not proof that this vessel was destroyed.
The symbols express Cesare's inarticulate shock; distinguish deliberate source comedy from an encoding defect.
The source explicitly identifies Rafael Castor of the Castor company. Preserve Rafael and the FO substitution.
Good Luck is a carved inscription offered and checked as evidence, not a ship name or new farewell.
Clau is familiar address for Claudio, not a family relationship; Gerhard's same-scent metaphor denotes kindred character, not literal smell.
meanings: Cesare again wonders where his エリュシオン号 has gone.
Gerhard worries about the pirate capture: such ships are generally stripped of gold and cargo and abandoned.
Cesare is distressed by that possibility.
A crew member reports a recent sighting of the ship near Lisbon.
Gerhard reacts in surprise.
Cesare is astonished that his ship may be nearby.
Gerhard proposes searching the harbor.
In the repeat-search variant, he proposes searching the harbor again.
Cesare agrees.
The search has failed here too.
Gerhard urges Cesare not to despair and assures him they will find it someday.
Charles also offers help.
It should at least be nearby; Gerhard says the rest depends on luck and urges hope.
Cesare quietly acknowledges this.
Gerhard has found nothing and asks Cesare about his side of the search.
Cesare emits inarticulate, symbol-rendered shock.
Gerhard asks what is wrong.
Cesare stammers the ship's name and cries that this is エリュシオン号.
Gerhard asks whether he has really found it.
Charles thinks so: Cesare ran aboard that ship making strange cries.
Under Claudio's source heading, Claudio asks whether this intruder is a thief.
Under Rafael's source heading, Rafael reacts to the report of a thief.
Under Cesare's source heading, Cesare calls the ship's name.
Charles observes that the situation has become a commotion.
Gerhard realizes they must stop Cesare and calls to him.
He repeatedly tells Cesare to calm down.
Cesare apologizes: seeing the ship made his mind go blank.
Claudio demands to know what is happening.
Rafael introduces himself as Rafael Castor of the Castor company and asks who they are.
Gerhard apologizes and introduces himself as Gerhard Adernkatz of {MACRO:FO}.
Rafael recognizes the well-known {MACRO:FO} name.
Gerhard introduces Cesare Tony.
Cesare apologizes for losing control.
Another member of Rafael's party asks why he boarded this ship.
Cesare says it is エリュシオン号 and used to belong to him.
Claudio rejects the claim because it is their ship now.
Rafael asks Clau to wait because Cesare's claim may be true.
Reminds the others that they found it as an abandoned ship washed onto the shore.
The other crew member asks whether there is anything to prove the claim.
Gerhard asks Cesare whether any evidence comes to mind.
Cesare remembers something.
He carved Good Luck on the side of the ship, and the marks should still be there.
The crew member asks Claudio to inspect the ship's side.
Claudio complains about being sent on the errand.
The truth must be established; the crew member challenges his standing as a man if he grumbles over such a small task.
Claudio agrees while complaining about being ordered around.
He returns incredulous: the inscription really is carved there.
Cesare asks eagerly whether it was found.
Charles celebrates the success.
Gerhard congratulates Cesare.
Cesare responds with relief.
The crew member realizes what this means about the ship.
Claudio is troubled because it has now become indispensable to them.
Gerhard acknowledges their position and asks what Cesare wishes to do.
After a pause, Cesare proposes leaving; seeing his ship again is enough.
He asks its present crew to take good care of it.
Charles addresses Cesare sympathetically.
Gerhard asks whether he is sure.
Cesare agrees.
Rafael stops them and confirms that this was Cesare's ship.
Cesare qualifies that it belonged to him once.
Rafael tells him to take エリュシオン号 back.
Claudio protests that this is a whole ship and asks what will become of their party.
Rafael says they will manage somehow; he understands Cesare's feelings and asks that they return it.
Claudio sighs at Rafael's excessive kindness but agrees.
Cesare asks whether they truly mean it.
Rafael confirms and says he will leave the ship tied at this dock.
Cesare thanks him, delighted to be able to travel with his ship again.
Charles congratulates him.
Gerhard also thanks Rafael and admires such generosity in someone so young.
Rafael demurs modestly.
Gerhard tells him not to be modest; he recognizes the same spirit as in his own admiral.
He says he is proud to have met Rafael and bids farewell.
Cesare gives heartfelt thanks again.
